solutions.check: 30 entries; each light the paper's grid did not give solved here from its clue's wordplay (an anagram or hidden word, the one listed word fitting every crossing) and its definition (WordNet), as the answer another puzzle gave the same clue, or as the one past answer its crossings left that the printed letters allow, agrees with the 29 answers the paper printed

clue.text: There are no waves in the river kind

definitions.text: There are no waves in the river kind

parts.words: There are no waves in the river kind
parts.note: hair can be wavy, but the river sort are the canal-and-river gates where water lies still, so no waves there

explanation.surface: A remark about calm stretches of river water.
explanation.walkthrough: The word also means tresses of hair, which may be waved; the river kind are gated chambers where boats are raised and lowered on still water.
explanation.definitionFit: River gates enclosing a still chamber for raising boats are the river kind, as opposed to hair.

clue.text: Greeks ? Then take me as Caledonian

indicators.note: take as here means work the letters into another form, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A Scot is invited to pass himself off as a Greek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take' signals a rearrangement of ME AS CALEDONIAN, all fourteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spartans of ancient Lacedaemon were a Greek people, so the plural names Greeks.

parts.note: reads like a warning to beware the sharp edge, but means the goods (ware) a knife-maker sells

explanation.surface: A warning to watch out for something sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ware' looks like 'beware'; it is ware as in merchandise, the knives and forks made by a cutler.
explanation.definitionFit: Knives, forks and spoons are tableware, much of it sharp-edged.

parts.note: reads as a question about the close of a performance, but says the word for a spectacle ends with the letters of How

explanation.surface: Wondering how a performance comes to a close.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for a spectacle is the letter S followed by HOW, so it literally ends in 'How'.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectacle is a public display or performance, an exhibition put on for viewers.

parts.note: a wake-up bell in a military camp would be an odd reveille, normally sounded on a bugle; split differently it is a Scottish surname

explanation.surface: An odd way to wake a Scotsman.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as CAMP BELL it is a camp's bell, an unusual reveille; whole, it is a Scottish clan name.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish clan surname, so a member of it is a Scot.

parts.note: the Cam is the river that flows through Cambridge
Brian is a man's name

explanation.surface: A man from a river in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Cambria is the old Latin name for Wales, so its adjective means Welsh.

definitions.meaning: a seaport on the south coast of Spain
a sweet fortified Spanish wine named after that port, akin to sherry

explanation.surface: A port wine served instead of a sherry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like the wine; it is the Andalusian harbour city, whose fortified wine is sherry-like.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andalusian city is a harbour and gives its name to a fortified dessert wine.

parts.note: cells hold prisoners; the cells of the mind hold thoughts

explanation.surface: Something that locks up thoughts like a jailer.
explanation.definitionFit: Neurons, the units of grey matter, are where thoughts are held, pictured as jail cells.

parts.note: the passing of moisture out through pores, as from leaves or skin

explanation.definitionFit: Transpiration is moisture escaping through pores, a seeping out of fluid.

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters could be put another way, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Journeys made without changing gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' signals that TRIPS IN ONE GEAR, all fourteen letters, is rearranged; the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Peregrinations are long journeys or wanderings, trips made from place to place.

parts.note: a single moth larva whose name has the letters of the word two inside it

explanation.surface: A greedy caterpillar eating two others.
explanation.walkthrough: The name holds T-W-O in its middle: CU, then TWO, then RM.
explanation.definitionFit: A moth larva that cuts through plant stems at ground level is a caterpillar.

parts.note: sounds like clothing for a walk in the forest, but means the foliage that clothes the trees

explanation.surface: What to wear for a forest walk.
explanation.definitionFit: Foliage clothes trees, so leaves together are the dress of woodland.

indicators.note: any way here means in either direction, so the word reads the same backwards and forwards

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A shrug that something is finished regardless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anyway' looks like 'regardless'; it means the word reads either way, forwards or backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An act or exploit is a thing done, so the noun fits something that has been done.

clue.text: This needs a ship and plenty of time

definitions.text: This needs a ship and plenty of time

parts.note: a brig is a two-masted sailing ship
an age is a long time

explanation.surface: A project requiring a vessel and lots of time.
explanation.walkthrough: Piracy and plunder do need a ship and time, so the clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Brigandage is banditry or plunder, the trade of robbers by land or sea.

clue.text: Such voices they had in Rome!

definitions.text: Such voices they had in Rome!

parts.words: Such voices they had in Rome!
parts.note: evokes great orators of Rome; the adjective comes from a loud-voiced herald in Homer

explanation.surface: Admiring the powerful voices of Roman orators.
explanation.walkthrough: Stentor was the herald in the Iliad whose voice was as loud as fifty men's; Roman orators addressing crowds needed such lungs.
explanation.definitionFit: Named after Homer's herald Stentor, the adjective describes an extremely loud, booming voice.

indicators.note: for here means in exchange for, so the letters are traded into a new order

explanation.surface: Offering someone a very small peg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' signals that A TINY PEG is rearranged; 'him' is a man from the land of the Nile.
explanation.definitionFit: A man from the land of the pharaohs, referred to by the pronoun him.

parts.note: a single fine layer laid over a surface, as of wood or paint

explanation.surface: A single light layer of paint.
explanation.definitionFit: A veneer is a thin surface layer of fine wood glued over cheaper material.

clue.text: What the horse does with them

definitions.text: What the horse does with them

parts.words: What the horse does with them
parts.note: a horse with the disease of that name lurches about, doing the same as the illness is called

explanation.surface: Asking what a horse does with something.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural noun is a disease of horses; a horse suffering it lurches, so it does the verb with the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A disease of horses causing a lurching gait, and also what such a horse does.

parts.note: a cook weeps while chopping these bulbs, not from grief

explanation.surface: A chef crying over something.
explanation.definitionFit: Chopping these pungent bulbs releases a compound that makes the eyes water.

parts.note: a gap-fill quotation from Shelley's The Witch of Atlas, completing the line about her clothing

explanation.surface: A line of Shelley's poetry with its last words missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in The Witch of Atlas runs 'A lovely lady, garmented in light / From her own beauty'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing two words complete Shelley's line, picturing the lady clothed in radiance.

parts.note: sounds like a bet placed entirely on one runner, but the letters of its first three words make a male horse

explanation.surface: A punter staking everything on one runner.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of IT'S ALL ON, put in another order, spell the answer: a male horse.
explanation.definitionFit: An uncastrated male horse, kept especially for breeding.

definitions.meaning: a police constable is in the police service, the force

explanation.surface: Checking a police constable's credentials.
explanation.walkthrough: P.C. is Police Constable, the lowest rank in British police.
explanation.definitionFit: A rule that is valid is currently operative; a constable is likewise within the police.

indicators.note: after places the word here behind the era abbreviation

parts.note: AD, Anno Domini, marks the present era, the years of our day
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to stay put from now on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts HERE behind AD, the abbreviation for the present Christian era.
explanation.definitionFit: To stick is to cling or hold fast, the same as to cleave to something.

parts.note: Barking is an east London district near this peninsula on the Thames; dogs bark, so barking is near them too

explanation.surface: Noise is heard close by somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a district of east London, a few miles from the Thames peninsula in Docklands with this name.
explanation.definitionFit: A Thames peninsula in east London's Docklands, a short distance from Barking.

parts.note: the four letters that start the clue, f-i-n-d minus some, rearranged; take it as a phrase of two short words, from the letters of fit and o

explanation.surface: A request to spell out a short word.
explanation.walkthrough: A two-word phrase of two letters each; the clue as held gives no firm mechanism, so it is read as a cryptic hint.
explanation.definitionFit: A common two-word phrase, as in 'make the best of it' or 'the long and short of it'.

clue.text: It travelled from China to Peru

definitions.text: It travelled from China to Peru

parts.words: It travelled from China to Peru
parts.note: echoes Johnson's line 'Survey mankind from China to Peru'; the primate imitates mankind everywhere

explanation.surface: Something that journeyed across the globe.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Johnson's poem The Vanity of Human Wishes opens 'Let observation with extensive view, Survey mankind from China to Peru'.
explanation.definitionFit: A primate, or a mimic; this one copies human ways the world over.

parts.note: informal dress, the word given in French spelling

explanation.surface: Casual clothes as worn by the French.
explanation.definitionFit: A light, loose informal gown or negligee worn indoors, the word borrowed from French.

parts.note: reads as a kind of harbour; a sort of the word seaport, its letters jumbled, makes a coarse grass

explanation.surface: A kind of harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: The seven letters of SEAPORT, sorted differently, spell the name of a coarse Spanish grass used for paper and rope.
explanation.definitionFit: A tough grass of Spain and North Africa, used to make paper, rope and baskets.

clue.text: Drill order not difficult to obey

definitions.meaning: a parade-ground command allowing soldiers to relax their posture
an order to stand at ease is an easy one to follow

explanation.surface: A sergeant's command that is simple to follow.
explanation.definitionFit: On the parade ground the command lets soldiers relax from attention, an easy order.

definitions.meaning: Brown ... was the nickname of the British Army's flintlock musket
a woman's name, short for Elizabeth

explanation.surface: Describing a woman whose colouring matches an old gun.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown Bess was the British Army's standard flintlock musket for over a century.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's pet name for Elizabeth, and with 'Brown' the nickname of the old army musket.
